name: Road-dust drain filter
subtitle: a storm drain that eats tyre particles

effects.effect: bacteria found at a recycling plant make an enzyme that breaks PET plastic apart
a learned model predicts a protein's 3D shape from its sequence
vent bacteria live on chemicals, without light or oxygen

effect: bacteria found at a recycling plant make an enzyme that breaks PET plastic apart
how: Tyres shed more microplastic than any other source, and one of the chemicals that washes off them kills salmon within hours of a rainstorm. This drain insert slows the first flush of a storm in a chamber packed with a bed of microbes chosen and fed to attack rubber and its additives, with designed enzymes doing the first cuts. The runoff that continues to the river has lost the fraction that does the killing.
obstacle: Rubber is a cross-linked network, far harder to cut than polyester, and a cold drain gives an enzyme little time.
why: Rubber-degrading microbes are slow; the need and the location are both real.
real: Stormwater inserts that retain tyre particles and 6PPD-Q exist (biochar/woodchip filter socks, permeable pavement, bioretention with >97% retention of particle-bound 6PPD-Q) and soil studies show 6PPD-Q degradation is microbially mediated with ~14-day half-lives, but no filter seeds or feeds microbes/enzymes to degrade tyre rubber in the drain.
